Question: How do recycled aggregates (RAP, RCA, steel slag) and supplementary cementitious materials change workability, strength gain, and long-term durability?
Method3: Research demonstrates that recycled concrete aggregate (RCA) and reclaimed asphalt pavement (RAP) can serve as sustainable alternatives to virgin aggregates in pavement subgrade and base layers. Stabilizing low-quality RCA with fly ash and Portland cement significantly enhances subgrade strength, stiffness, and shrinkage properties, with economic benefits realized when these combinations are used together[1]. Field evaluations indicate that blends of RCA and RAP (specifically a 60–40% mix) perform satisfactorily as improved subgrades, with minimal rutting under load, while 100% RAP layers may suffer from greater deformation[2]. Studies on Portland cement treated bases show that increasing cementitious binder content improves durability, and RCA can match the performance of virgin aggregates, though freeze-thaw durability criteria may need adjustment for D-cracked aggregates[3]. The use of unconventional recycled aggregates is viable for low-volume and unsurfaced roads, but careful control of blend ratios and compaction is crucial to mitigate deformation and ensure long-term performance[2]. The addition of SCMs (supplementary cementitious materials) such as fly ash or slag further enhances performance by improving long-term hydration, reducing microcracking, and mitigating volumetric instability. This is supported by experimental evidence showing reduced length change and microstrain in SCM-modified mixtures, indicating enhanced dimensional stability and durability under cyclic moisture and temperature variations [4]. Method3: Research on interaction techniques for virtual and augmented reality has made strong progress in using tangible and context-aware tools to enhance user performance and engagement. Tangible user interfaces (TUIs) that use augmented reality (AR)—for example, physical props tracked via ARToolKit in CAVE systems—enable intuitive 3D manipulation and navigation, allowing seamless transitions between one- and two-handed operations while reducing dependence on tethered devices (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/30836). In scientific data analysis, high-fidelity VR systems and gesture-based techniques like the Volume Cracker improve the usability of 3D volume visualizations, with studies showing how system fidelity affects task performance (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/51817). Educational AR systems for young STEM learners combine computer vision and machine learning to create engaging, hands-on learning experiences and support human–AI collaboration (https://hdl.handle.net/1903/26840). Context-sensitive frameworks also support dynamic mapping across input devices in distributed environments, maintaining interoperability and responsiveness (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/27940). Finally, hovercast slider menus for 3D object interaction showcase more fluid and adaptive approaches to virtual manipulation (Figure Link; https://hdl.handle.net/10919/83948). Collectively, these advances reflect a shift toward more natural, adaptive, and effective interfaces in immersive VR and AR systems.

Question: How have AI tools helped people analyze data more easily, especially those without strong programming skills?
Method3: A wide range of AI-driven tools now make data analysis and application development easier for people without strong programming backgrounds. Block-based programming tools for Alexa Skills, for instance, let even elementary school students create conversational AI applications, narrowing the gap between technology consumers and developers [https://hdl.handle.net/1721.1/122704]. In data analysis, spreadsheet tools remain the most widely used platform, combining data storage, programming, and debugging in a familiar environment [https://doi.org/10.7275/10678415.0]. For educators, frameworks such as SimBuilder allow teachers to design and adapt educational simulations without coding expertise, promoting exploratory learning in K–12 classrooms [https://hdl.handle.net/10919/28766]. In genomics, workflow systems like BioFlow offer web-based interfaces for visually designing and managing complex pipelines while supporting error tracking through audit logs [https://hdl.handle.net/10919/24809]. Visual analytics tools also help users explore and interpret high-dimensional data, as demonstrated in medical imaging [https://digitalcommons.wayne.edu/oa_dissertations/685]. Collectively, these innovations show how AI tools are becoming more intuitive and inclusive, empowering broader participation in data analysis and development.
Method2: AI tools have made data analysis more manageable for individuals without strong programming expertise, primarily through structured interfaces and simplified visualization systems (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/48422, https://hdl.handle.net/10919/70950, https://hdl.handle.net/10919/28766). Visual analytics tools with object-level interactions allow limited manipulation of model parameters and basic exploration of high-dimensional datasets, helping users observe outcomes rather than perform in-depth analysis (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/70950). Frameworks designed for reuse and learning within visual programming environments have been developed to assist novice users, particularly educators, in building and modifying educational simulations, though their functionality often remains confined to small-scale tasks (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/28766). Similarly, block-based programming tools for Alexa Skill creation have lowered the technical entry barrier, enabling inexperienced users, including children, to construct simple conversational AI programs without genuine understanding of the underlying logic (https://hdl.handle.net/1721.1/122704). These systems have reduced the technical difficulty of interacting with AI systems but have not eliminated dependence on pre-defined tool structures or templates. Research indicates that interactive analysis tools can support surface-level data exploration and limited insight generation, even when users lack advanced computational skills (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/70950). Overall, while AI tools have made data analysis more accessible and visually guided, they mainly promote usability over analytical depth, leaving expert-level interpretation largely unchanged.

Question: What challenges are documented in applying machine learning models to limited supervision or noisy datasets?
Method3: Recent research has significantly advanced the development of machine learning models capable of handling noisy, incomplete, or corrupted datasets, particularly in high-dimensional and unstructured contexts. One key direction has been the design of algorithms that exploit the multi-dimensional structure of signals, rather than treating noise and missing information in isolation. By leveraging the inherent structure in the data, these models can improve classification and representation performance even when labels are unreliable or information is missing [https://digitalcommons.wayne.edu/oa_dissertations/2166]. Deep learning methods, especially convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have shown state-of-the-art results on visual object recognition tasks but are often hindered by the need for large, clean labeled datasets. Semi-supervised and robust training approaches have been proposed to address label scarcity and noise, enabling models to learn effectively from limited or noisy annotations [https://digitalcommons.wayne.edu/oa_dissertations/2026]. In addition, strategies such as weak supervision, outlier filtering, and hybrid approaches combining deep and traditional methods have demonstrated improved robustness and scalability for both classification and representation tasks in corrupted environments [https://etda.libraries.psu.edu/catalog/9484]. Further, research has addressed non-convex optimization challenges arising from data perturbations, developing perturbation-aware algorithms that maintain generalization and reliability in the presence of adversarial or random data corruption [https://hdl.handle.net/1721.1/127004]. Finally, practical advances in outlier detection and integrity checks—such as the Deep k-Nearest Neighbors classifier—provide mechanisms for identifying unreliable predictions, thereby enhancing the trustworthiness of machine learning models applied to noisy or adversarial datasets [https://etda.libraries.psu.edu/catalog/15065ngp5056].
Method2: The application of machine learning models to limited supervision or noisy datasets is a challenging task, and several studies have documented the challenges and proposed solutions to address them (https://hdl.handle.net/1853/47700, https://hdl.handle.net/2142/110579, https://hdl.handle.net/2142/107972, https://etda.libraries.psu.edu/catalog/17131azs5955, https://etda.libraries.psu.edu/catalog/23319). For instance, the lack of training data and the complexity of narratives in news article datasets make it difficult to apply traditional text classification methods, and weakly supervised classification methods that rely on class name semantics may not be effective (https://hdl.handle.net/2142/110579). Additionally, the use of noisy metadata in scholarly big datasets can lead to incorrect indexing and retrieval, and machine learning models may struggle to learn from such data (https://etda.libraries.psu.edu/catalog/17131azs5955). Furthermore, the privacy risk in machine learning systems is a significant concern, and attacks on models can reveal sensitive information, making it essential to develop protection mechanisms that balance privacy and data utility (https://hdl.handle.net/2142/107972). The development of improved generative modeling approaches for semi-supervised and domain adaptive classifier learning can help address these challenges, and methods such as stochastic data generation and space-partitioning can lead to better classification performance and generalization on unseen data (https://etda.libraries.psu.edu/catalog/23319). However, the lack of a suitable syntactic representation for machine learning problems and solutions can limit the development of mechanized and automated statistical and algorithmic principles, making it difficult to experiment with customized statistical models and alternative algorithms (https://hdl.handle.net/1853/47700). Overall, these studies highlight the need for further research and development of methods and techniques that can effectively address the challenges of applying machine learning models to limited supervision or noisy datasets.

Method3: Integrative approaches, such as consensus combination and inconsistency detection, have been developed to improve classification accuracy and anomaly detection by combining both labeled and unlabeled data from diverse domains. These methods enable actionable knowledge extraction even when traditional single-source learning would fail, as demonstrated in applications ranging from social network analysis to cyber-security and business intelligence [https://hdl.handle.net/2142/29822]. Knowledge transfer and sharing are particularly crucial when data is scarce or incomplete, requiring both supervised and unsupervised techniques to avoid negative transfer and bias while boosting generalization [https://digitalcommons.wayne.edu/oa_dissertations/829]. Information fusion frameworks utilizing kernel methods, fuzzy integrals, and genetic programming have shown that fusing evidence from multiple sources—such as sensor data, algorithms, and human input—yields more robust and accurate results compared to single-source models, especially in scenarios with noisy or limited data [https://doi.org/10.37099/mtu.dc.etdr/375][https://hdl.handle.net/10919/28198]. Mixture-of-kernels and composite kernel mapping approaches further allow automated learning of the relative importance of each data source, enhancing interpretability and reducing the need for extensive manual labeling [https://hdl.handle.net/10657/3675]. As illustrated in Figure [Figure Link], hybrid models that combine traditional and machine learning algorithms can further optimize performance by integrating complementary strengths [https://hdl.handle.net/1853/60768]. Collectively, these findings underscore the power of multi-source and knowledge-transfer strategies in overcoming data limitations, improving classification, and enabling scalable, domain-agnostic machine learning solutions.

Question: How has parallel programming evolved to support modern high-performance computing systems?
Method3:
Programming heterogeneous parallel and approximate computing systems presents significant challenges due to the diversity of hardware architectures, parallelism models, and memory hierarchies. Recent research addresses these complexities by proposing new abstractions and compiler frameworks for improved portability and performance. One notable approach introduces HPVM, a hierarchical dataflow graph-based intermediate representation that captures parallelism across various hardware and supports both functional and performance portability. Its extension, ApproxHPVM, enables accuracy-aware performance and energy tuning by translating application-level accuracy constraints into hardware-specific requirements, facilitating dynamic scheduling and efficient offloading to accelerators while maintaining user-specified accuracy levels (https://hdl.handle.net/2142/104762). Complementary work explores high-level programming languages and compilation techniques, such as leveraging Chapel and StarPU, to map computations efficiently onto emerging architectures like GPUs, with compiler-driven heuristics for optimizing nested parallel loops and providing portable machine characterization (https://hdl.handle.net/2142/45443).
Further advancements include frameworks for transparent GPU virtualization, enabling applications to utilize distributed GPU resources as if they were local, thus supporting GPU-as-a-service paradigms and live migration for load balancing (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/51845). Another line of research develops runtime systems like MPI-ACC, which extend familiar programming models to automate data movement and task mapping across CPUs and accelerators in clusters, improving both productivity and cluster utilization (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/52366). Additionally, template-based static optimization frameworks in C++ demonstrate that concise, pattern-driven code can achieve performance on par with optimized C on multi-core CPUs, balancing productivity, performance, and portability (https://hdl.handle.net/2142/49466).
Collectively, these innovations underscore the importance of compiler and runtime support, high-level abstractions, and virtualization in democratizing access to heterogeneous parallel computing, improving programmability, and achieving scalable, portable performance across diverse systems.
Method2: Parallel programming has evolved significantly to support modern high-performance computing systems, with various frameworks and techniques being developed to improve productivity, performance, and portability (https://hdl.handle.net/1853/52985, https://hdl.handle.net/1853/54431, https://hdl.handle.net/2152/33304, https://hdl.handle.net/2142/49466, https://hdl.handle.net/2142/49427). For instance, speculative parallelization has been explored as a means to efficiently utilize many-cores with minimal programmer effort, with techniques such as feedback-driven concurrency control and algorithmic speculation being developed (https://hdl.handle.net/1853/52985). Additionally, high-performance instrumentation frameworks have been designed to collect and represent parallel programs, enabling a deeper understanding of dynamic aspects of programs and optimizing compiler optimizations (https://hdl.handle.net/1853/54431). Furthermore, managed languages and virtual machine technologies have been optimized to exploit hardware heterogeneity and parallelism, achieving high performance, energy efficiency, and portability on evolving parallel hardware (https://hdl.handle.net/2152/33304). Template-based static optimization and library-driven optimization have also been developed as programming frameworks to achieve a good combination of productivity, performance, and portability, allowing developers to write concise code that achieves close-to-optimal performance on a wide range of parallel machines (https://hdl.handle.net/2142/49466, https://hdl.handle.net/2142/49427). Overall, these studies demonstrate the significance of parallel programming in supporting modern high-performance computing systems, and highlight the importance of developing frameworks and techniques that can efficiently utilize parallelism, optimize performance, and improve productivity.

Question: What are the reported challenges in ensuring trustworthy NLP for healthcare applications?
Method3: Ensuring trustworthy NLP for healthcare applications involves tackling challenges in data quality, model reliability, and contextual understanding. Traditional “knowledge-lean” statistical models, while effective for many NLP tasks, often fail in domains requiring deeper contextual or encyclopedic knowledge. By leveraging large unlabeled corpora, Wikipedia-derived knowledge, and logical constraints, researchers have demonstrated improvements in tasks such as named entity recognition, information extraction, and coreference resolution, showing that knowledge-rich approaches can outperform conventional methods [https://hdl.handle.net/2142/31198]. In the medical domain, NLP plays a key role in extracting patient information from electronic health records (EHRs) and clinical notes, though issues such as data heterogeneity and noisy terminology persist. Advanced models like translation-edit and attention-based reasoning support automatic question answering and clinical event prediction within EHRs [https://hdl.handle.net/10919/104711]. Comparative evaluations of NLP algorithms for medical texts reveal that variations in annotation standards can cause inconsistent results, highlighting the need for improved fidelity in clinical concept extraction [https://hdl.handle.net/1721.1/100298]. Beyond healthcare, research on adversarial attacks and model integrity identifies vulnerabilities in deep learning systems and suggests using integrity checks to enhance robustness and interpretability [https://etda.libraries.psu.edu/catalog/15065ngp5056]. A visual comparison between traditional and smart healthcare illustrates the growing impact of integrated NLP and machine learning in modern clinical environments [Figure Link, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc1157532/].
Method2: The reported challenges in ensuring trustworthy NLP for healthcare applications include the need for robust adaptation to language variation, handling of unstructured and noisy clinical texts, and ensuring the trustworthiness of logging and event-based probing mechanisms (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/104711, https://hdl.handle.net/1853/58201, https://hdl.handle.net/2142/92849, https://hdl.handle.net/1721.1/100298, https://hdl.handle.net/1721.1/119754). For instance, language variation in clinical texts can lead to poor performance of NLP systems, and techniques such as text normalization and domain adaptation are needed to overcome these challenges (https://hdl.handle.net/1853/58201). Additionally, the use of event-based probing mechanisms can help detect attacks and system hangs, but ensuring the trustworthiness of these mechanisms is crucial (https://hdl.handle.net/2142/92849). Furthermore, the comparison of different NLP algorithms for medical texts highlights the need for standardized evaluation metrics and datasets to ensure consistent and reliable results (https://hdl.handle.net/1721.1/100298). The application of NLP to precision clinical diagnostics and treatment also requires careful consideration of the trustworthiness of the output, particularly when using deep learning and machine learning methods (https://hdl.handle.net/1721.1/119754). Overall, these studies demonstrate the importance of addressing the challenges of trustworthy NLP in healthcare applications to ensure accurate and reliable results, as discussed in the references provided (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/104711, https://hdl.handle.net/1853/58201, https://hdl.handle.net/2142/92849, https://hdl.handle.net/1721.1/100298, https://hdl.handle.net/1721.1/119754).

Question: What technology solutions have been developed to reduce digital inequity for low-resource communities?
Method3: Technology solutions aimed at reducing digital inequity for low-resource communities emphasize participatory design, affordability, and contextual relevance. One study developed the Respectful Space for technology typology, a framework grounded in oral traditions and underrepresented narratives to ensure that digital systems amplify marginalized voices while preserving cultural agency and ownership (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/103473). Building on this, another long-term engagement in Nepal demonstrated how assets-based socio-technical systems can empower trafficking survivors by leveraging existing community strengths instead of external interventions, promoting self-determined, sustainable reintegration through inclusive co-design practices (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/104635). Addressing inequities in digital literacy, research on digital security education revealed that fragmented and inconsistent online materials disproportionately disadvantage under-resourced users, calling for unified, accessible, and evidence-based approaches to bridge the digital safety divide (https://hdl.handle.net/1903/25404). Another line of work explored the role of social media and computing infrastructures in supporting asylum seekers and undocumented migrants, showing how technology facilitates coordination, advocacy, and care networks while highlighting design failures that marginalize these humanitarian efforts (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/99900). Finally, a project proposing a low-cost wireless Internet system for rural India used aging satellites and community-based Wi-Fi distribution to deliver affordable Internet connectivity to remote villages, offering a replicable model for resource-constrained environments (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/42495). Together, these studies demonstrate that addressing digital inequity requires more than infrastructure—it depends on culturally grounded, community-driven, and socially aware technological design.
Method2: Several technology solutions have been developed to reduce digital inequity for low-resource communities, including amplifying underrepresented stories, improving social interaction in local community organizations, creating online communities, and developing low-power communication systems (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/103473, https://hdl.handle.net/10919/32741, https://hdl.handle.net/10919/45436, https://hdl.handle.net/10919/33579, https://hdl.handle.net/1853/47814). For example, the "Respectful Space" framework has been developed to amplify underrepresented stories and ensure that technology design respects the agency and ownership of these stories (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/103473). Additionally, research has been conducted on the effect of technology on social interaction in local community organizations, highlighting the importance of considering how technology can be used to aid social interaction in these settings (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/32741). The concept of community has also been explored in the context of synchronous computer-mediated communication, highlighting the potential for online communities to exist and thrive in low-resource settings (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/45436). Furthermore, research has been conducted on rural income and wealth inequality in China, highlighting the need for technology solutions that can address these disparities (https://hdl.handle.net/10919/33579). Finally, low-power communication systems have been developed to enable multi-gigabit communication in low-resource settings, with applications in mobile communication devices and other areas (https://hdl.handle.net/1853/47814). Overall, these studies demonstrate the potential of technology to reduce digital inequity and improve the lives of individuals in low-resource communities.
